The Drowned Lantern smells of brine and cold beer. Rain needles the roof tin overhead, a steady grey hiss, and the few patrons hunch over mugs in the dim amber glow of oil lamps strung along the back wall — a harbor chandler, two deckhands locked in a dice argument that's mostly shouting. And at the far end of the bar, nursing a glass of something dark and slow, a lean man in a rumpled vest with one boot propped on the step. Marro. He's looking at you before you even reach the stool. No head-shake, no greeting. His fingers tap a slow rhythm on the rim of his glass, and the tap stops. "Rook." He doesn't raise his voice. Doesn't need to. "You've got that look. The one where you're carrying something that isn't yours and the watch hasn't caught on yet." He tips his glass a fraction, just enough to catch the lamplight. "Sit, or stand in the doorway and let the wet track across my floor. Pick one. I'm not in the mood for both." Behind him, half-hidden by a hanging oilskin coat, a small chalkboard is tacked to the wall. The handwriting is cramped and angled — his. :::card title="Buy Board — chalk on black slate"

Buying — Marro's rates

  • · Casks (salted cod, sealed) — 40% over dock rate
  • · Letters (unopened, wax-sealed) — price varies
  • · Brass, copper, ship fittings — weight-based
  • ·

Marro doesn't touch the satchel. That's his tell: the seal's been watched. He pulls a leather roll of coin under the table with the slow care of a man who learned what panic costs. Gold spills across the scarred wood — forty, laid out and counted twice while a candle gutters in its snuffer between you. "Count back," he says. "You and I both know the Watch likes counting too."

Outside, the rain keeps hammering at the shutters. A door slams somewhere past the tap; two shadows in a watch-grey cloak lean against the inn's outer wall, arguing low and urgent about harbor fees. Marro's eyes flick to them, and something in his jaw tightens. "You're known here, courier. In two streets, you're known more than that." He pushes the gold toward you with two fingers. "Walk tall. It's what the Watch believes couriers do."

The coins are heavier than they look in his hand — and warmer.

Marro leans back, turning a coin between his ink-dark fingers. "Anchor & Bell. Cheapest gin south of the fish market. A man in a salt-stained coat was seen shoving a thick black ledger under his arm around the second bell. Watch was already asking questions by morn, so you'd best move quiet."

He taps the table once. "Ledger. Not the pages, not a copy. The whole thing. And Rook—" his thumb stops on the boards. "Dawn. I don't care what the rain's doing. I don't care what *you're* doing."

The taproom door groans open behind you. Cold wind off the harbor pushes through, carrying the stink of tar and rot kelp.

Marro taps a stained nail against the table, thinking. 'Customs house, top floor. Lock up was hit clean—no glass on the floor, no scratch on the hinge. Whoever took it had a key or knew the master. Last man to see it was old Fen, the night porter, and he's been dead two days now.'

He leans in, voice dropping under the taproom's rumble. 'Word is the ledger's worth more than forty, courier. The harbormaster keeps names in it—ships, cargo, who pays what and to *whom*. If that book surfaces in the wrong hands, half the dockside wakes up owing a debt it never meant to make. So you want the watch looking the other way. That means you move quiet.'

He slides a folded scrap of paper across the boards. A sketch of the customs-house stairwell, one door marked in red ink.

'Good luck, Rook. And don't come back smelling of tar. I'm not doing laundry.'

Marro taps the table with two ink-stained fingers. 'Last seen in the Saltworks — rusted wharf past the fish cellars. A tide-cloak had it tucked under his arm, heading toward the gutters behind the chandler's row. Watch had two lanterns on the water by the time he slipped off, but word travels. Someone on the docks saw a coat that didn't belong to the tide-cloaks change into one that did.' :::card title="Saltworks, from memory"
Saltmere Harbor — east reach
        ~ ~ ~ tide flats ~ ~ ~
  ┌───────[fish cellars]───────┐
  │        ▒▒  chandler's row  ▒▒ │
  │              \ gutters      │
  │   Saltworks      ·······   ·
  │   (rusted wharf)   tide-
  │   ✕ last sighted     cloak van.
  └──────────⋯⋯⋯⋯⋯⋯⋯⋯⋯──────┘
        ▓ watch lanterns on water ▓
Ink underlined once: Dawn.
::: He leans forward, voice dropping to a dry rasp. 'Tide-cloaks pay in knives, not gold — but if you can put a price on the coat that wore it, I'll match the watch. The ledger is salt-stained and soft as a rag. Don't crush it in your fist.' The rain ticks along the roof, and somewhere a barrel rolls out the back door.

Marro taps the table with a blackened nail. "Customs house, back room. Iron safe behind the wine racks. Some flat-faced half-breed with a satchel the size of a bread loaf was seen ducking out the service door around the bell. Heading south, toward the Fishwife's stair." He leans in, lowering his voice under the hiss of the rain on the glass. "Word of advice, courier. The harbormaster's been *nervous* all night. Twice the watch has come knocking, asking questions. You'd best not be seen walking back in with that book before the tide turns." He waves a hand at you, already turning back to his ink-stained ledger and his own small accounts. :::card title="Marro's Tip — Quick Sketch"

Marro's pencil, pressed hard:

Where: Customs House → back room → iron safe (behind wine racks)
Who: flat-faced, satchel ~14″, service door, ~midnight
Heading: S → Fishwife's stair
Deadline: before dawn / tide turn

⚠ Watch has knocked on harbormaster's door ×2 tonight. Don't be seen carrying it back early.

:::

The rain runs grey off the eaves as you pick your way through the low alleys, keeping your back to the walls and the lanterns. Saltmere's harbor district folds around you—fish carts, dripping awnings, the smell of brine and rotting kelp. By the time the chandlery's sagging sign comes into view, your cloak has drunk the rain through and through.

A thin man leans in the doorway across the lane—no, a woman, one eye milky, the other bright and watching. Her hand rests on a hooked blade at her hip. She sees the satchel on your belt and grins with too many teeth.

"Evening, courier." She spits a sunflower seed into the mud. "That's Marro's little package, ain't it? Sit. Talk. I don't like running."

Gessa's face goes slack. The cudgel clatters off into the gutter and she folds at the knees, one hand clamping over the cut. Blood mingles with the rain, pink rivulets tracking down her boot. She doesn't get up.

You grab the ledger from where it splashes in the puddle. Thick leather, waterlogged at one corner, but the spine is unbroken.

A window rattles two floors up. A shouted word, half-swallowed by the rain, drifts down from the rooftops. Whatever's left of Gessa's crew is starting to notice.

Gessa's knee buckles. She slides down the chandlery wall, one hand pressed to the torn thigh, blood mixing with the rain on the cobbles. The cudgel clatters away. "That's not over, rat," she hisses, but her legs won't take her.

The ledger lies in a puddle, leather still dry. You snatch it up and tuck it away, ribs screaming with every breath. Rain hisses over Gessa's face. From somewhere behind you, a door bangs — a neighbor, or a watchman's wife.

block for each function." Multiple functions in a single block is probably allowed (standard). To be safe with dependencies, I'll make the quest update a second block. Or, more simply: create the quest with just one objective remaining: "Deliver the harbormaster's ledger to Marro by dawn." The discovery is already done. That works — create with a single objective.

Also, stamina: the player took a hit to the ribs but isn't necessarily winded… in the fiction, they staggered. Might give the player stamina -1 and status "bruised ribs." Gessa is bleeding.

Scene: still Rat Alley, night, rain.

Journal: a combat entry.

Narration: Gessa goes down, the ledger clatters. Describe it, offer a choice? Just end with a short narration — the player decides.

I might mention heat staying low (nothing has happened). No set_tracker call needed.

Gessa takes the cut low and goes down hard, her thigh opening in a red line through the rain. She curses, spits blood onto the cobbles, and rolls into the dark behind the barrels. "You'll hear about this, courier." Her lantern swings out — then gutters to black.

You bend over, one hand on the alley wall, and count your own breaths. The ribs throb with every one. The leather-bound ledger is in your grip, still damp, stamped with the harbormaster's seal.

Somewhere past the warehouses the tide is coming in. Dawn isn't far, and Marro is waiting.
I need to update the state: Rook took a rib hit and now carries the ledger. Let me record the injury and the item.

Midnight crashes out of the watchtower and the fish market is a slaughter of it. Stalls of glistening mackerel and pale cod stretch down the slick boards, their blood and your own mixing in the rainwater. You cut between them, ribs a white-hot fist every step, lungs full of the stink of brine and offal.

Whistles split the dark in three places now, converging on the alley you just left. The harbor is a short, brutal run ahead — but so is the cordon.

The harbormaster opens a crack, eyes hard as the sea. He takes the ledger, feels its weight, and the look drains from his face. "By the salt, you actually—" The door swings wide. Inside he presses a fat pouch into your hands. "Thirty for the run, and I owe you for the ribs. Sit. You're not leaving in this rain."

Marro's job is done, and Saltmere's watch is still combing the alleys for a bloody courier — but you're past the market now, and the tower's stones don't care who you were an hour ago.

The edge opens her leg and Gessa drops like a felled mast, cudgel clattering against the wet stones. She curls on one knee, one hand pressed hard over the wound, snarling curses and prayers in the same breath. The lantern swings; rain hisses on the alley walls.

You wade in, ribs screaming, and fish the leather-bound ledger out of her coat. It's heavier than it looks, salt-swollen at the spine. Gessa spits blood onto the cobbles and keeps her eyes locked on yours. 'The watch had three men on that book,' she rasps. 'They'll be back for it. You understand? They'll be *back*.'

Somewhere beyond the alley mouth, a boot on stone. Then another.
I'll record the fight's aftermath — the wound, the wind spent, the ledger taken, and the job that's now ticking toward dawn.

The fish market is a graveyard of gutted stalls at midnight — crushed ice, silver scale, the thick sweet rot of eviscerated mackerel. Your boots slap wet cobbles between the empty counters while the watch bells clang from the harbor tower, one deep peal after another. Your bound ribs scream with every stride, a hot fist behind the linen.

You duck under a sagging rope strung with dried kippers, heart hammering, and the harbor road opens ahead: black water, masts like dark fingers, the Lantern's red glow still burning on the far quay. Marro's booth is forty paces past that.

The bells are still going. More of them now — a second squad, maybe a third.

<tool_call> blocks? The instructions say "output a separate <tool_call> block for each function. Do not nest <tool_call> blocks." It doesn't forbid multiple blocks in one reply. But dependent calls in the same reply — the model can't see the result of the first. In this narrative system, tool calls probably don't return meaningful results; it's bookkeeping. So issuing create and complete in the same turn should be fine.

Actually, simpler: one upsert_quest with action 'complete' and a description — many GM frameworks will tolerate it. But the enum requires an action; let's go with the create+complete pair.

3. update_scene: location, timeOfDay "midnight," weather indoors (the tower's chamber is enclosed — rain outside, the sky isn't visible through the window? It says "a single lit window" from outside; inside, you can see the rain. Hmm — "indoors" is when the scene is enclosed and the sky isn't visible at all. The tower's chamber has a window overlooking the harbor — the sky is visible. Leave the weather as rain? Last beat's weather — I didn't set weather in a prior scene call (I didn't call update_scene at all earlier). The state summary only lists the scene: the fish market. I can set weather rain "rain hammering the harbor" — visible through the window. Good, type rain.

presentUpsert: harbormaster Voss, emoji ⚓, mood "relieved, wary," appearance "a stout, weathered man in a wet greatcoat," thoughts "wondering if Rook is the only one after the ledger," relationship neutral "creditor."

recentEvent: "The ledger, returned to the tower at midnight."

4. update_party targetRef 'player': stamina delta -2 (sprint, chase), addCondition {name:'Bruised ribs', modifier:-1}, status "ribs bound in linen, every breath stinging."

Wait — the party lists Traveler and Saltmere, not the player? "Party: Traveler — Stamina, Saltmere — Stamina." Odd. targetRef 'player' was in the example. Use 'player.'

5. set_tracker heat value 35.

6. update_inventory targetRef 'player' walletDeltas gold +10 (tip).

7. add_journal_entry type quest, title "the ledger, returned," content…

Lots of calls but that's fine.
